justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline trajectory, with prices drifting slightly higher from a current level around 158 over the course of the forecast horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 158.5 is essentially flat, reflecting mean-reversion tendencies in equity prices over very short windows and the absence of any specific scheduled catalysts that would drive a large directional move. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate marginally higher to 159, acknowledging a slight positive drift embedded in historical equity returns while recognizing that a week is still a short enough window that noise dominates. At the one-month horizon, the 161 estimate reflects a more meaningful incorporation of that long-run positive drift, roughly consistent with annualized equity returns of mid-to-high single digits applied over a 30-day window.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which follows directly from the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility. At one day, a range of roughly plus or minus 4 points reflects typical daily realized volatility for a mid-to-large cap equity or ETF in this price range. By one week, that range roughly doubles to plus or minus 8 points, and by one month it widens further to plus or minus 16 points, consistent with monthly volatility estimates in the 10–15% annualized range. These widths are also informed by the general macroeconomic environment, which has featured above-average uncertainty around interest rates, inflation readings, and central bank policy communications.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise inflation print or Federal Reserve policy shift that materially reprices interest rate expectations, which could produce a gap move well beyond the one-day interval in either direction. Earnings announcements, if this is an individual stock, could easily produce a 5–10% single-day move that breaks through the stated bounds. Geopolitical escalation, a credit event in the banking sector, or a significant deterioration in economic data could produce tail outcomes well outside the one-month interval.

More broadly, my intervals assume a relatively stable volatility regime. If realized volatility were to spike — as it does during risk-off episodes — the true distribution of outcomes would have fatter tails than my stated intervals imply. Conversely, a period of unusually low volatility or strong macro clarity could compress realized outcomes within a tighter range than I've specified. Liquidity conditions and broader market sentiment shifts are difficult to quantify but represent genuine sources of model error at all three horizons.
